data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The fetch budget must be dual-denominated in both requests and bytes, with exhaustion triggered by whichever limit is hit first. This eliminates the weaknesses of single-denomination approaches: a requests-only budget fails to control data volume, and a bytes-only budget fails to control API call frequency. Only a dual budget provides complete resource control and auditability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The dual budget adds complexity, but it is necessary to cover both dimensions of resource consumption.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent uses caching, cache hits must be accounted for in both dimensions: a cache hit counts as a request (if it would have been a fetch) and as virtual bytes equal to the cached response size.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The atomicity of the dual check must be ensured, e.g., via a mutex or compare-and-swap.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The agent is configured with a request limit R and a byte limit B. It maintains two counters: requests_made and bytes_transferred. Before each fetch, it checks if requests_made + 1 > R or if bytes_transferred + estimated_fetch_size > B (using a conservative estimate if exact size unknown). If either condition is true, it terminates with a typed terminal state indicating which limit was exceeded: 'request_budget_exhausted' or 'byte_budget_exhausted'. The terminal state includes both current counters and the budget limits. The check is atomic to handle parallel fetches. Retries count against the request budget, but a separate retry allowance can be configured.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
